youtube.baslik: School-Age Hearing Screening | Lesson 176 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Why and how are school-age children screened for hearing loss? In this lesson we cover the first-grade screening program in Türkiye, the 20 dB HL pure-tone screening protocol, the role of tympanometry, and the rescreening and referral criteria.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: American Academy of Audiology, Childhood Hearing Screening Guidelines (2011); American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, Guidelines for Audiologic Screening (1997); Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Health, School-Age Children Hearing Screening Program; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn why hearing screening is done in school-age children and how it is carried out.
Step by step, we will cover the pure-tone screening level, the role of tympanometry, and the rescreening and referral criteria.
Even in a child who passed newborn screening, a loss can begin later or progress.
Some of these losses go unnoticed until the child starts school.
Mild and unilateral losses are easily missed in children who understand speech well in a quiet setting.
In the preschool and early school years, middle ear fluid, or otitis media with effusion, is common.
This fluid is often temporary, but when it lasts long, it can affect listening and learning in class.
In older children and teenagers, noise-related high-frequency changes may also appear.
School screening aims to catch these losses, unnoticed by teachers and families, before their effects in class grow.

ogeler.metin: At the start of primary school

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, the Ministry of Health has run school-age hearing screening with the Ministry of National Education since 2016.

cumleler: The program covers first-grade primary school students in public and private schools.
Screening is done at school by trained health staff, using a portable device and a play-based approach.
The program's detailed protocol, screening level and referral rules are set out in the Ministry's current program documents.
Before screening, parents receive an information note, give consent and fill in a short questionnaire about the child's hearing.
In this lesson, we will build on the shared principles of international guidelines.
The American Academy of Audiology's 2011 childhood screening guideline also defines the minimum grade levels to screen.
Preschool, kindergarten and first grade top this list; middle ear problems are more common at these ages.
The guideline also recommends screening in later primary grades, for example in third and fifth grade.
At least one more screening is recommended in middle school or high school.
These levels are the minimum; programs may screen more often depending on their resources.
For older students, screening high frequencies is also recommended when screening is combined with hearing conservation education.
Any child whose teacher or family has a concern is evaluated regardless of the screening schedule.
At school age, the core method is pure-tone screening; guidelines recommend it from about three years of age.
With a screening audiometer and supra-aural earphones, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz are tested in each ear.

cumleler.yazi: In the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, or ASHA, and American Academy of Audiology guidelines, the level is 20 dB HL.
cumleler.ses: In the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, or ASHA, and American Academy of Audiology guidelines, the level is twenty decibels HL.

cumleler: Screening does not look for a threshold; it checks whether the child hears the sound at this single level.
If the child does not respond, the same tone can be presented again up to four times.
If there is no response at any frequency in either ear, the result is recorded as refer.
In young children, play responses, such as dropping a block into a box on hearing the sound, are more reliable than raising a hand.

cumleler.yazi: Let us see what the screening level catches on this example audiogram; the green zone extends down to 20 dB HL.
cumleler.ses: Let us see what the screening level catches on this example audiogram; the green zone extends down to twenty decibels HL.

cumleler: The right ear thresholds are inside the green zone at all tested frequencies, that is, better than the screening level.

cumleler.yazi: This ear hears the 20 dB HL tones and passes the screening.
cumleler.ses: This ear hears the twenty decibel HL tones and passes the screening.

cumleler.yazi: In the left ear, however, there is a threshold of 35 dB HL at 4000 Hz.
cumleler.ses: In the left ear, however, there is a threshold of thirty five decibels HL at four thousand hertz.

cumleler.yazi: This child will not hear the 20 dB HL tone at 4000 Hz and so does not pass the screening.
cumleler.ses: This child will not hear the twenty decibel HL tone at four thousand hertz and so does not pass the screening.

cumleler.yazi: Some programs use 25 dB HL because of room noise, but 20 dB HL catches mild and high-frequency losses better.
cumleler.ses: Some programs use twenty five decibels HL because of room noise, but twenty decibels HL catches mild and high-frequency losses better.

cumleler: Remember, in screening we do not know these thresholds; this audiogram is an example made only to show the logic.

maddeler.metin: Poor at detecting middle ear fluid

cumleler: Schools are not sound-treated booths; classroom and hallway noise masks low frequencies the most.
So a missed response at 500 Hz may come from room noise rather than hearing loss.

cumleler.yazi: 500 Hz used to be added to screening to catch middle ear fluid, but it was found to be unreliable for this purpose.
cumleler.ses: Five hundred hertz used to be added to screening to catch middle ear fluid, but it was found to be unreliable for this purpose.

cumleler.yazi: In 1997, ASHA removed 500 Hz from its recommendations; tympanometry is a better tool for middle ear status.

cumleler: Programs may still add 500 Hz to suit their conditions; in that case, a quiet room is especially important.
Each screening day begins with a biological check showing that the device and earphones are working.

cumleler.yazi: Pure-tone screening can miss some middle ear problems, because fluid does not always cause a loss greater than 20 decibels.
cumleler.ses: Pure-tone screening can miss some middle ear problems, because fluid does not always cause a loss greater than twenty decibels.

cumleler: So guidelines recommend adding tympanometry to pure tones, especially for preschool, kindergarten and first-grade children.
In a healthy middle ear, the tympanogram shows a clear peak; this is called type A.
When the middle ear is filled with fluid, the curve flattens; this flat curve is called type B.

cumleler.yazi: The American Academy of Audiology guideline recommends a tympanometric width above 250 decapascals as the refer criterion.
cumleler.ses: The American Academy of Audiology guideline recommends a tympanometric width above two hundred fifty decapascals as the refer criterion.

cumleler.yazi: If the device does not report width, static admittance below about 0.2 mmho can be used as a second option.
cumleler.ses: If the device does not report width, static admittance below about zero point two millimhos can be used as a second option.

cumleler: According to the guideline, negative pressure alone is not a reason for referral.
Tympanometry is also used as a second-stage test for a child who did not pass pure-tone screening.
A child who did not pass pure-tone screening is rescreened right away, with the earphones repositioned and the instructions repeated.
The reason for not passing is often a misplaced earphone or not understanding the instructions.
A child who also does not pass the rescreen gets tympanometry.
If pure tones are not passed but the tympanogram is normal, the loss may be sensorineural; the child goes to audiology without waiting.
The guideline clearly stresses that these children should not wait for a rescreen.

cumleler.yazi: A child who did not pass both pure tones and tympanometry is rescreened 8 to 10 weeks later.
cumleler.ses: A child who did not pass both pure tones and tympanometry is rescreened eight to ten weeks later.

cumleler: This is because middle ear fluid often clears on its own within this time.
A child who does not pass this second screening either is referred for medical and audiological evaluation.
Programs may use a more intensive rescreening and referral protocol, depending on their resources.
The screening day starts with a biological check of the device; its annual calibration must also be up to date.
The quietest room in the school is chosen for screening; if possible, doors and windows are kept closed.
The child is first taught how to respond, using an audible practice tone.
Presenting tones in a regular rhythm, or looking at the child while presenting a tone, makes responses predictable.
So the intervals between tones are varied, and the child is seated so they cannot see the device controls.
The result is recorded separately for each ear and frequency.
The family is informed in writing of the result and the next step, and completion of the referral is tracked.

sahneler.metin: When a child does not pass, first check earphone placement, the ear canal and the instructions. But do not look for excuses to explain the result away.
cumleler: A tip from the field: for a child who did not pass, first check the simple causes.
Check whether the earphone sits fully over the ear, and whether hair or an eyeglass arm is in the way.
Explain the instructions again in shorter words, or through play.
But if the child still does not pass after these checks, do not try to explain it away as shyness or daydreaming.
The protocol exists for exactly these children; the referral decision is made according to the protocol.

maddeler.metin: School screening finds new, mild losses

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that school screening aims to catch new, progressive, mild and unilateral losses.

cumleler.yazi: In pure-tone screening, 1000, 2000 and 4000 Hz are tested in each ear at 20 dB HL.
cumleler.ses: In pure-tone screening, one thousand, two thousand and four thousand hertz are tested in each ear at twenty decibels HL.

cumleler: In preschool and the early grades, tympanometry is also added, and it is used as a second stage for children who do not pass.
A child who did not pass pure tones but has a normal tympanogram is referred for audiological evaluation without waiting for a rescreen.

sahneler.soru: A child refers on pure tones; the tympanogram is normal. Next step?
sahneler.aciklama: If the middle ear is normal, the loss may be _sensorineural_; there is no waiting.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: a child did not pass the pure-tone rescreen, and the tympanogram is normal. What is the next step?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: refer for audiological evaluation.
Since the middle ear is normal, the loss may be sensorineural; these children do not wait for a rescreen.
